title: Is this crazy-looking home sauna just what our busy daddy reporter needs in his life?
description: Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home. Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. Now, though, he’s got a wife and kid, plus an apartment out in the suburbs that’s closer […]
content:
Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home.

Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. Now, though, he’s got a wife and kid, plus an apartment out in the suburbs that’s closer to the mountains than the office, and thus a long commute, leaving him with only enough time for one or two sauna days in an entire year.

So in his quest for the optimal sauna/life balance, he decided to purchase a home sauna.

Converting an entire room of his home into a sauna facility would be excessive in terms of cost and floorspace, so instead of doing that he went looking for a home sauna kit on Rakuten, where he found an assemble-it-yourself steam sauna kit for 17,780 yen (US$112). All of the components shipped together in a large cardboard box, and Ahiruneko laid them out to see what he’d be working with.

Folded up inside that cloth pouch is the material for the sides of the sauna tent, pictured with it in the above photo are a floor mat, piping for the tent’s frame, one device for producing steam, another for dispersing it inside the tent, and a hose to connect them.

Also included in the set were a folding chair and one of those rollers that are supposed to stimulate the pressure points on the bottom of your feet to provide various vague wellness benefits.

The included instructions were written in less-than-fluent Japanese, but between them and the photos on the Rakuten product page here, Ahiruneko could figure out what he needed to do. He started by removing the tent material from its pouch and assembling the pipe frame.

This was a pretty quick and simple process, and before long the tent was standing in the middle of his living room.

It almost looks like a giant down vest, with a slot for your neck and also two little slits that you can open if you want to reach your hands outside the tent.

There’s also an exterior pocket where you can keep the remote control to turn the steam generator on and off or adjust the temperature.

Speaking of the steam generator, it resembles a rice cooker.

You fill it with water, and once the liquid gets hot enough to start turning into steam, it gets channeled through the side of the tent by the connecting tube…

…and dispersed by the steam box, which you place inside the sauna with yourself.

The dimensions of the tent are cozy, but there’s room to spare in which to fit the chair, and laying down the mat before your steam session will help keep your floor from getting damp.

OK, with everything assembled, it was time to turn ono the steam generator! Ahiruneko hit the power button…and had no idea what the display said.

That blurriness isn’t from Ahiruneko’s camera. His brand-new home sauna’s display was foggy and indistinct, almost like it was censoring itself with a mosaic. Luckily, the control buttons all had legible labels, and the printed instructions had told Ahiruneko that once steam started coming out of the top of the sauna tent, it was ready for him to step in.

It took about 20 minutes for the steam to heat up, but when it did, entering the tent turned out to be surprisingly tricky, since the frame has a pair of connected pipes running horizontally across the front. Ahiruneko ended up having to temporarily pull them apart, step inside the tent, and then put them back together.

Now that he was finally inside, all he needed to do was zip the front back up…

…and settle in for a steam session.

If you’re setting one of these up for yourself, you’ll definitely want to give your housemates a heads up beforehand, so that they don’t wander into the room and think you’ve been decapitated, or maybe had your body from the neck down converted into machinery in order to become a sauna cyborg.

But as startling as this setup looks when viewed from the outside, it was extremely relaxing for Ahiruneko on the inside. He’d purposely kept his expectations low about how high the temperature could get, but it turned out that the steam filling his home sauna was surprisingly hot. It wasn’t long until his body was sweating steadily, but his head being exposed kept the environment from feeling stifling or even stuffy.

In time, though, Ahiruneko started to sweat from his face too, so he unzipped one of the arm holes so he could grab the remote control and turn down the temperature just a bit.

He’d actually put a second remote control in the pocket too, the one for his TV, since having his own personal sauna means he can watch whatever he wants while staming.

As for negatives, the device that emits steam inside the tent does, understandably, get very hot, so you do need to be conscious of where it’s placed and make sure not to step on it. You also need to wipe down the tent and let it dry before you fold it back up, which adds a little time and hassle to the start-to-finish process.

Still, even with some cleaning up to do, Ahiruneko is still coming out ahead, time-wise, by being able to have a sauna session without having to leave his home. He thinks he’ll still probably look for opportunities to treat himself to a trip to a professional sauna when he has the chance, but for those times when his schedule or budget is tight, he’ll be very happy to use this at-home version again.

title: 10 of the nicest celebrities we’ve met in Japan over the years

content:
Who wowed our reporters the most with sheer friendliness?

Our website has been around for quite a while now, and over the years we’ve even had the opportunity to rub shoulders with famous movie stars and musicians from time to time. Considering we’re known for behavior that some may deem “gross” or “indecent,” it wouldn’t be too shocking if they treated us like the schlubs we admittedly are, but there have been a few who really seemed to shine as genuinely good people.

So, our Japanese language writers would now like to take a moment and give credit where credit’s due to the famous people from Japan, as well as famous people from abroad who visited Japan, who really made a positive impact on us.

When it comes to celebrity interviews, P.K. Sanjun is usually our frontline reporter. As such, he’s met the likes of Will Smith, Arnold Schwarzenegger, and Tom Holland, to name a few. But here are the people who made the biggest impression on him.

● Chris Pratt

I’ve interviewed a lot of Hollywood actors, and they’ve all been really nice. I sort of think you need to be in order to make it out there.

But among them, Chris Pratt stood out as a super nice person. When I finished my interview, I was just sitting there feeling awkward, but he took the initiative and said, “Hey! Let’s take a photo together!” It was a god-tier gesture and made me fall in love with the guy.

View this post on Instagram

● Maximum the Ryo-kun

He’s a very private person. You could even say he’s mysterious, and very artistic too. But he’s also an absolute legend and totally down to earth when you talk to him. So much so that I found myself wondering, “Does a celebrity like this actually exist?”

The rest of the band [that he’s in, Maximum the Hormone], were great too. Nao-chan immediately snapped a picture after Ryo-kun shaved my eyebrows. Even though it’d been years since I last interviewed them, Daisuke-kun greeted me with a friendly “Long time no see!”

Of course, Ue-chan, who shyly chatted with me about kendama, was wonderful too. In short, Maximum the Hormone aren’t just great because of their music. They’re a class act as well.
If I ever get another chance to meet Ryo-kun, I want to ask him why he loves [’80s Japanese rock band] Lindberg so much.

View this post on Instagram

Mr. Sato’s been known to do a few interviews in his days as well, including none other than Santa Claus. But what big names managed to out-nice even Ol’ Saint Nick for our star reporter?

● Cunning Takeyama

I’ve met the famous Japanese comedian Cunning Takeyama a few times now, and every time his genuine kindness shines through. His work often involves interacting with the general public in TV segments, so he seems to make a conscious effort to make people feel at ease. That gentle, approachable character he shows the moment he meets someone is something that I aspire to emulate as an adult.

View this post on Instagram

● Shinichiro Azumi

I’ve been invited on his TBS radio show Nichiyo Tengoku a few times. Even though it’s a live broadcast, he went out of his way to look after me because of my lack of experience in this setting. He has a way of completely managing the flow of conversation but never lets it show by drawing stories out of me naturally. It’s the mark of a true professional and made a strong impression on me in the way I could relax and have a natural conversation with him.

You don’t often see Yoshio interviewing famous people, unless it involves a money-making scheme,  but he’s often behind the camera at these meet-ups and has interacted with plenty of famous people as well. Here’s who made the biggest impact on him.

● Matt Damon

I was a photographer at an interview with him during the release of Jason Bourne. He might be a world-famous actor, but he didn’t act like it at all and answered every question from P.K. with sincerity. I’ve been present for a lot of celebrity interviews, but Matt Damon was the nicest of them all. It really took me aback how humble someone of his stature could be. He was just a very cool guy.

● Yumi Adachi

I was the photographer when Seiji interviewed her while pretending to be Yngwie Malmsteen. I always thought she had a very elegant fashion sense and way of life, so I was intimidated to meet her, but she turned out to be incredibly friendly and cheerful, exactly like she is on television. While we were standing around waiting, she noticed I had the latest iPhone at the time and said, ‘Wow, it’s got three lenses!” I still have and cherish that phone to this day.

▼ Yumi Adachi and Yngwie Malmsteen (Seiji Nakazawa)

The interviews where Seiji Nakazawa pretended to be Yngwie Malmsteen in an effort to join famous people’s musical projects were always dicey ones. They rarely ended up being actual interviews, and the famous people involved would have had every right to chew us out for making a mockery of the whole process. But it’s also a chance for celebrities to really show how easy-going they can be, as Ahironeko recalls.

● Non

This was our very first Yngwie project, and I was the photographer. The awkward tension in the air was so thick both for us and the people on her side. None of us really knew what was going on.
Considering that, it wouldn’t have been a surprise if she just snapped at us with, “Excuse me… What the hell are you doing?” But she was all smiles the whole time. A true goddess.

View this post on Instagram

Takashi Furusawa is a newer addition to our staff and hasn’t been to as many interviews as the others. But that doesn’t mean he hasn’t had his own brushes with greatness.

● Miki Narahashi

Miki Narahashi is best known as the voice of Misae Nohara in the long-running hit Crayon Shinchan.
But for me, she was also my senpai when I was at voice acting school. I still clearly remember how she always looked out for me, giving me advice and kind encouragement when I had problems.
It was a true honor to have studied under her for two years, and I still cherish that experience to this day.

▼ Nararhashi has played the mother of Shin-chan for the entire run of the series.

As Takashi mentioned, not all of our celebrity encounters come from interviews. Many of our writers have also appeared on TV and radio over the years, where they’ve bumped into famous faces. Go Hatori has a few memories along those lines too.

● Kuroda

I met Kuroda, from the comedy duo Messenger, when we appeared together on a TV show in Osaka in 2014 and I was asked to talk as a spam email expert. I was so nervous that my legs were shaking uncontrollably, but he kept tossing out these perfectly timed, light-hearted jokes that completely eased my tension. He had a way of making everything I said funny and was just a truly kind and thoughtful person. I’m filled with both gratitude and admiration for him.

● First Summer Uika

I met First Summer Uika (a singer, actress, and media personality) while doing voice acting and on some TV sets. She was always very approachable and easy to talk to. It left a big impression on me! One time she even came all the way from her dressing room to where I was working to say hi. I’m such a big fan of hers now that I even have an acrylic standee of her on my desk. I even have a T-shirt with her on it that I’ve kept secret until now.

title: This Tokyo snack shop can send your taste buds on a trip around Japan for just 1,000 yen
description: There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo. In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would […]
content:
There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo.

In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would require, but there is a way to send your taste buds on a trip across Japan for a very affordable price, as we found out on a recent visit to the Marui Annex department store in downtown Tokyo’s Shinjuku neighborhood.

On the first floor of the building you’ll find a shop named Edited Japan Shinjuku, which just opened in September . “Edited” isn’t being used with the meaning of revising or altering something, though, but more in the sense of an “editor’s selection,” as Edited Japan is a curator of Japanese regional sweet and salty snacks. The store is stocked with over 100 different items, representing all of Japan’s prefectures, and unlike some food souvenir shops that only offer large-quantity boxes, Edited Japan specializes in individual-serving sizes, letting you pick out a variety of treats without making any major commitment as you search for a new favorite.

Another cool thing about Edited Japan is the store’s focus on snacks that are a genuine part of everyday life in their local communities. You won’t find anything that’ll win you brownie points with a snooty coworker or snobby classmate here. Instead, the shelves are filled with things that present a combination of high quality and reasonable price. Think more “This is something people in Kyoto would munch on if they want something sweet on a Sunday afternoon” than “Bring this to the next party you’re invited to so you can show off your refined sensibilities.”

So we decided to see how many prefectures’ treats we could taste with a budget of 1,000 yen (US$6.30), and we mean a hard limit of 1,000 – not a single yen more.

Thankfully, this still gave us plenty of room to work with, since most of Edited Japan’s items are somewhere in the 100-200 yen range. We had to do some mid-shopping calculations to make sure we didn’t go over, but in the end, we were able to put together a bundle of snacks from six different prefectures, with the total coming to 995 yen.

So what did we get? Let’s start at the north of the country, and work our way down, which makes our first entry on the list Hokkaido Dining Kitchen’s Corn Soup (130 yen), from Hokkaido Prefecture.

Soup may not be counted as a “snack” in some cultures, but certain varieties in Japan do sort of get treated that way. Corn pottage, for example, is commonly seen as something that’s tasty and moderately filling even when it’s not served as part of a meal, which is why you’ll often see cans of corn soup for sale in Japanese vending machines during the fall and winter. This powdered corn pottage mix, though, is tastier than what you can get from a can, as it’s made with an especially sweet variety of Hokkaido-grown corn and contains no artificial flavors or preservatives.

Next have Dutch Senbei rice crackers, from Yamagata Prefecture’s Sakata Beika, which were the value all-star of our shopping trip, priced at just 45 yen.

This brand of rice cracker has been a big hit in Yamagata since 1962, but what makes them “Dutch,” other than the cap that person is wearing in wrapper illustration? There are two theories, one of which is that the distinct bumpy texture of the crackers is said to resemble the footprints left by visitors from Japan to the Netherlands, some of the first foreigners to set foot on Japanese soil back in the feudal era, and thus some of the first people to be seen walking around in Western footwear, which was much bulkier than the straw sandals that were the norm for Japanese people at the time.

The other possible explanation is that Oranda, the Japanese word for both Holland and Dutch, sounds similar to orada, a way of saying “we” in the Yamagata dialect, which would make “Oranda Senbei” (as the snack is called in Japanese) sound similar to saying something like “the rice crackers we made.”

Regardless of why they’re called that, though, Sakata Beika’s Dutch Senbei are crisp and refreshing, lightly salted to enhance, but not replace, the natural flavors of the non-glutinous Yamagata-grown rice that they’re made with.

Next we move on to Kyoto, which means it’s time for nama yatsuhashi.

Nama yatsuhashi is a folded triangle of soft mochi with a dollop of anko (sweet red bean paste) inside. Chewy and sweet, with just a touch of sophistication from a dusting of cinnamon, nama yatsuhashi are so popular with Kyoto residents and visitors that there are a few different companies that make them. Nishio, who makes the 250-yen matcha-flavored version we picked up, is one of the most respected, because if your company has been around since 1689, you’ve earned a lot of trust.

Since nama yatsuhashi’s simple ingredient list lends itself well to experimentation, most makers, Nishio included, have a cycle of seasonal flavors that are only offered at certain times of year, but the matcha ones are so well loved that they’re available pretty much all the time, as long as the day’s stock isn’t sold out.

Continuing west, our taste buds arrive in Hyogo Prefecture, where the coastal town of Akashi brings in some of the country’s most delicious octopus, inspiring rice cracker maker Eirakudo to make Akashi Takosen senbei (250 yen).

These deep-fried senbei are made with Akashi octopus and treated with a savory, slightly sweet sauce, and they’re just as suited for a midday snack as they are for a pairing with a nice cold beer after work.

We shift back into sweets mode as we reach Hiroshima Prefecture, which, like Kyoto, has a particular dessert that’s overwhelmingly associated with it: the momiji manju.

Hiroshima Prefecture is famous for its beautiful maples, called momiji in Japanese, and these manju (sweet dumplings) are shaped like the trees’ leaves.

The outside is a sponge cake similar in flavor and texture to a dorayaki or castella cake, and while the most traditional filling in anko, momiji manju come in all sorts of different flavors, and we opted for a custard cream version from maker Yamadaya, from the island of Miyajima, for 180 yen.

And last, we come to the end of our sweet pseudo-odyssey in Ehime Prefecture with the linguistically dense Shiki Hamu Anpan Manju (140 yen), from confectioner Ichiroku.

We’ve already covered the meaning of manju, and anpan is a hybrid dessert of a western-style baked bread bun with anko inside. Hamu is an old-fashioned/literary way of saying “eat” in Japanese, and the Shiki being referred to here is Masaoka Shiki, a 19th century poet who’s considered one of the greatest haiku masters in Japanese history.

Masaoka was born in Ehime, and is also said to have been a big anpan fan. So while this is still a manju, the cake is a little more substantial, and it’s crowned with black sesame seeds, a common addition to anpan.

We were a little bummed out that we weren’t able to fit some snacks from Kyushu or Okinawa into our taste buds’ itinerary, but we really can’s complain after enjoying six different delicious desserts for just 1,000 yen, especially when we got a taste of so many different parts of the country. Now that we’ve got the snack-travel bug, we’ll have to make sure to swing by Edited Japan whenever we’re in the neighborhood but also kind of wishing we could be someplace else.

title: Mochido donuts make a squishy return to Lawson stores across Japan
description: Mochido or Mochidon’t. There is no Mochitri. Earlier this year, we stumbled upon a pair of donuts sold by convenience store chain Lawson that completely redefined the genre of convenience store donuts. They were called Mochibee (Mo-chee-bay), and came in powdered sugar and roasted soybean (kinako) flavors. Though they tasted delectably sweet, the whole experience […]
content:
Mochido or Mochidon’t. There is no Mochitri.

Earlier this year, we stumbled upon a pair of donuts sold by convenience store chain Lawson that completely redefined the genre of convenience store donuts. They were called Mochibee (Mo-chee-bay), and came in powdered sugar and roasted soybean (kinako) flavors. Though they tasted delectably sweet, the whole experience was a bittersweet one because this was just a limited trial run, and Mochibee weren’t sold nationwide.

But our writer Natsuno Futon was delighted to hear that Lawson have finally gotten their act together and re-released these treats all over Japan, starting on 20 October. However, the name has changed to Mochido, perhaps because the “beh” part of the name led people to think they were bagels instead of the similarly shaped donuts.

Hoping only the name was different, she hurried to her nearest Lawson on the evening of the 20th, only to find they were already sold out.

Unsure if they were really that popular already or if her timing was just unlucky, she decided to give up for the night but was able to find them the next morning. The same flavors of sugar and kinako were there, and Futon picked up one of each. The price was just the same as before: 171 yen (US$1.10) each.

At a glance, they looked exactly the same as she remembered them, with their slightly irregular shape a testament to their chewy fluffiness and a gracious coating of sweet powders. 

Futon decided to start with the plain sugar, and after cutting off a piece, it seemed to have that same layered texture as before. She reminisced about that delightfully crisp surface, enhanced with cracker flour and poppy seeds.

Unable to hold out any longer, she popped a piece into her mouth and was immediately transported back to that blissful afternoon snack last March. It was every bit as good as it was back then, possibly even better somehow.

Next, she tried out the kinako flavor. Obviously, the texture was just as good here, but what really knocked it out of the park for this one was the perfect balance of kinako that made its presence known but didn’t overpower the innate deliciousness of the donut itself.

Both donuts had incredible attention to detail and seemed more like the kind you’d buy from a bakery rather than a convenience store. Futon was overjoyed after thinking she’d lost these treats forever after the last time.

However, she also crunched the numbers, and the calorie intake from these two decadent donuts far outweighed the calories burned during her 30-minute walk to and from the store. This imbalance would not bode well for her waistline, but thus is the life of a donut lover.

title: Chainsaw robots helping keep trains running safely in east Japan [Video]
description: Chainsaw-wielding robots prove they can contribute to human mobility in ways other than people running away from them in terror. Japan’s rail network is famous for its sterling safety and reliability records, and neither of those would be achievable without a whole lot of preventive maintenance. East Japan Railway Company (a.k.a. JR East), one of […]
content:
Chainsaw-wielding robots prove they can contribute to human mobility in ways other than people running away from them in terror.

Japan’s rail network is famous for its sterling safety and reliability records, and neither of those would be achievable without a whole lot of preventive maintenance. East Japan Railway Company (a.k.a. JR East), one of the nation’s largest rail operators, is constantly monitoring the condition of its tracks and carriages in order to spot potential problems before they occur, and when it spots an issue that needs to be addressed, it dispatches a crew to take care of it.

And sometimes some of the members of those crews are chainsaw-wielding robots.

JR East’s maintenance division had noticed that tree branches growing over the tracks near Nobeyama Station in Nagano Prefecture needed to be cut and cleared away, in order to keep them out of the way of trains traveling on this section of the Koumi line. To do so, they rolled out one of their new multifunction heavy railway machines, a humanoid robot attached to a vehicle capable of traveling on rails like a train or on streets like a truck. The robot’s left hand is a multi-pronged claw, suited for grabbing and moving branches and other debris, but where things get really awesome is the right hand, which is a chainsaw.

The robots appear to be updated versions of the units JR West started using in 2024. JR East began adding the robots seen in the above videos to its maintenance fleet in March of this year, but there have only been limited opportunities for the public to see them. The company has traditionally tried to schedule its maintenance projects for the middle of the night, so that they can be completed in the time between the last train of the night and the first of the morning, so as not to disrupt service for passengers. An increasing number of maintenance workers have been requesting day shifts, though, and the company is looking to accommodate them, which also affects the robots’ usage, since the machines are human-operated.

Online reactions to the JR East robot’s day at Nobeyama have included:

“All of a sudden, we’ve got the kind of awesome robots I’ve always dreamed about.”
“Yes! It’s so cool how the left and right arms are different.”
“Total R-O-B-O-T vibes.”
“It reminds me of the robot from [Studio Ghibli’s] Laputa.”
“Is this the robot that the T-800 Terminator is gonna get developed from?”
“So should we call this a ‘labor,’ like they call the mecha in the Patlabor anime?”
“Hey, didn’t I see that thing in Contra: Hard Corps’ train stage?”
“It’s a robot, but it’s also kind of cute.”

JR East says that shifting a greater number of maintenance projects to daylight hours will necessitate more frequent closures of line during their regular operating hours, but hopes that passengers will be understanding, and acceptance will most likely be easier to accept if they come with the promise of more chances to see robots in action.

title: 93-year-old Japanese grannie helps set trap for scam artist half her age
description: This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it. Over the past few weeks, Japan has seen a sharp spike in the number of data leaks and cyberattacks, with many organizations warning citizens that their personal information may have been compromised. So on October […]
content:
This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it.

Over the past few weeks, Japan has seen a sharp spike in the number of data leaks and cyberattacks, with many organizations warning citizens that their personal information may have been compromised. So on October 21, when a 93-year-old woman living in the town of Aisho, Shiga Prefecture, received a phone call from a man informing her that he was a police officer, and that there had been an unauthorized withdrawal of funds from her back account, it was cause for concern.

He did assure her, though, that because the problem had been detected quickly, they could remedy it in a swift manner too. The police would need her help to do so, though. First, he instructed her to freeze her bank account. Second, he said that the authorities would need to examine her ATM card, but to make that part of the process as convenient as possible for her, he said that he could send an investigator to pick the card up at her home. Finalizing that pickup time took a little extra conversation, with the woman talking to the man on the phone the next day as well, but eventually they agreed that the investigator would come that very day, October 22, to take come get the card.

Now, there are a number of warning lights that might be going off in your head right now. For starters, if there’s been some kind of anomaly with your bank account, it’s usually your bank that will contact you, not the police. Your bank will probably want to be part of the conversation too if you need to relinquish possession of your ATM card, and it’s also sort of unusual for the police to do house calls to pick up evidence rather than asking you to come down to the station.

So it’s pretty clear that the woman was the target of scammers. Unfortunately, this sort of scheme, taking advantage of senior citizens’ trusting nature and confusion regarding technology and bureaucracy, is a time-tested, reliable way of defrauding them, and the 47-year-old man who came to pick up the her ATM card was probably feeling smugly satisfied from proving his superior intellect compared to the befuddled woman.

However, the woman turned out to be far savvier than the fraudster had bargained for. She hadn’t been sitting in her living room wringing her hands between phone calls. She’d sniffed out that this was a scam, so she got in touch with the nearby Higashiomi Precinct of the Shiga Prefectural Police. She then pretended to have been fooled, but when the man pretending to be a police officer came to her house, there was a squad of real police officers already there, lying in wait, and instead of getting the woman’s ATM card, the man got arrested.

As he hasn’t entered a plea or gone to trial, yet, currently his arrest is for “suspicion of attempted fraud.” Honestly, though, of you show up at the door of an elderly woman who’s never met you before and tell her she needs to give you her ATM card, the only possible explanation other than fraud would be if you were robbing her, so things aren’t looking good for him from a legal standpoint either way.

It’s unclear whether the man who came to the woman’s home is the same man who’d called her on the phone, but police (the real police) believe that he was working with other criminals to set up the scam, so hopefully they’ll be apprehended as well, perhaps with the help of an equally large network of tough-as-nails grannies.

content:
Yakiniku Like wants to help diners get some likes of their own.

Japan has a lot of yakiniku restaurants, where you grill your own meat, but Yakiniku Like is different from the rest. Whereas typical yakinuku places have their grills set into table for a group of dining companions to gather around, all of Yakiniku Like’s seats are at counters, with an individual-size grill for every customer.

This setup, complete with your own personal selection of sauces and controls for the strength of your grill’s fire, makes Yakiniku Like the perfect place for solo diners who’re craving yakiniku, But just because you happen to be eating alone doesn’t mean you’re not a socially minded person, and so one of Yakiniku Like’s branches in downtown Tokyo has created a special seat specifically for customers who want to take photos and record videos of themselves to share on social media.

Situated in a corner of Yakiniku Like’s Shinjuku Minamiguchi branch, just a short walk from bustling Shinjuku Station, Studio Like, as the special seat is called is equipped with handy self-photography equipment such as a lighted vanity mirror for checking hairstyling and makeup, camera mounts for overhead filming, and a backdrop and surrounding walls to guarantee some extra personal space and for the benefit of other customers who’d rather not be featured in someone else’s pics or video clips. title: Japan’s mission to Martian moon and back underway
description: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing. At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this […]
content:
This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing.

At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this writing, all systems are operating normally.

▼ And was there ever any doubt that there’s also a cute mascot version of MMX?

The MMX’s mission is to travel to Phobos, one of Mars’ moons, land there, pick up samples, and bring them back to Earth. It’s one of the most ambitious Mars missions to date, but Japan’s space agency JAXA has already made a name for itself by landing on asteroids and returning samples successfully on two previous endeavors.

Considering Phobos is up to ten times the size of those asteroids and locked into Mars’ orbit, this might seem like an easier mission. However, the key factor is overcoming the gravity of both Phobos and Mars. The MMX will have to make a soft landing on Phobos, then take off again in order to return to Earth. As a result, about 68 percent of the spacecraft’s total weight is just propellant.

It is hoped that by collecting material on Phobos, we can learn more about how it and Mars’ other moon, Deimos, were formed. The two leading theories are that they were once asteroids that got captured by Mars’ gravity or that they formed from the debris expelled by a massive collision of something with the red planet. In addition, it is said that about 0.1 percent of material on Phobos is actually Martian soil, having been ejected when meteorites struck the planet. The goal of the MMX is to pick up at least 10 grams of material from Phobos for an estimated 0.01 grams of actual Martian material.

▼ Here’s a simulation of how it should all go down in a nutshell.

Whether this will be the first sample from Mars transported by humans back to Earth remains to be seen, however. China is currently preparing to send its Tianwen-3 to Mars, where it will collect 500 grams of pure Martian soil and bring it back to Earth. Both projects are scheduled to return here in 2031, so if everything goes as planned for everyone, it’ll be a relative photo-finish to see which country will be the first to break off a piece of Mars and carry it back.

Going according to plan is a big “if” as well. The MMX was originally expected to launch in 2024, but development of the H3 was delayed and the very tight window when Earth and Mars are properly aligned once every two years closed. China will also need to make sure everything progresses like clockwork from now until their launch in 2028 to avoid their own two-year delay.

Regardless of whoever does get back first, these samples will help to blow open our understanding of the Martian environment, including the possibility that life once or even still exists there in some form. Then, maybe we can finally get back to checking out our neglected other neighbor Venus someday.

It’d be pretty funny if all this time there actually were a bunch of aliens living in those boiling sulphuric clouds, wondering why no one ever comes looking for them.

content:
Refresh yourself with fruity sweetness while the crowds have yet to discover the store.

Japan’s cafe culture is a flourishing landscape of specialty roasters, themed cafes, and retro junkisssa coffeehouses. However, the presence of large foreign players, led by companies like Starbucks and Gong Cha, can’t be understated due to their expanding presence in the sector. Recently, a budget, large-capacity coffee brand from South Korea, Fave Coffee, has been opening locations one after another, while the world’s largest food and beverage chain Mixue from China is also steadily increasing its number of stores.

In this environment, B-Fresh, billing itself as “a brand from the Middle East,” has made its first splash into the waters of the Japanese market with  opening a store in Tokyo’s Harajuku neighborhood on October 1. Our ace reporter Mr. Sato was slightly worried it would already be bearing the brunt of the throngs of young people that flow through Harajuku’s streets, he still decided to give it a go.

About three weeks after the opening of the store, Mr. Sato stepped foot into Harajuku, and despite it being a weekday, Takeshita Street was crowded as usual, with places like Marion Crepes seeing no drop in customers regardless of day or time, with people lining up endlessly.

Scouring the streets, Mr. Sato was sure that he was in the right area and was keeping an eye out for one of these telltale lines, indicating a store’s popularity, but it turns out there was no line for B-Fresh at all.

This meant great convenience for Mr. Sato, but he lamented the fact that it had just opened and felt kind of desolate already. It may just be that word of mouth for the store hasn’t spread yet, and business will pick up in the weeks to come. On top of that, it looked as if the building is undergoing exterior wall construction, so if there hadn’t been a sign indicating they were open as usual (tsujodori eigyochu, 通常通り営業中), an uninformed passerby might assume they were not open at all.

The store itself is a juice bar that serves smoothies using fresh fruit, acai bowls, and yogurt, with a variety of items that Mr. Sato was unfamiliar with or unsure how to choose.

Using the ticket vending machine inside the store, Mr. Sato chose based on appearance and ordered something called B-Pink Brûlée, priced at 1,100 yen (US$7)] for a large (please note that only cashless payments are accepted in the store).

While waiting for his order, Mr. Sato inspected the menu some more. The products seem to be broadly divided into three categories: bubble drinks, smoothies, and acai bowls and frozen yogurt. The main representative of the bubble drinks is the Bubble Tea, and you can also choose fruit juice-filled pearls. For smoothies, there are drinks that blend things like Nutella and Oreos along with fruit, and toppings such as superfoods like chia and flaxseed can be added to any order. The range of customization really is quite wide.

In light of the numerous options and indecisiveness, Mr. Sato focused on which menu photos looked appealing, but seeing the actual drink itself, he was confident that his choice was not wrong as it looked incredibly delicious.

▼ Plenty of whipped cream and strawberry crunch on top

Making up the drink was a mix of strawberries, vanilla milk, and “creme brulee,” but even after drinking it, Mr. Sato wasn’t quite sure what the creme brulee was actually represented by—he believes it might be the custard cream.

The menu photo also showed strawberry pearls inside of it, but that was an additional topping for 100 yen, so Mr. Sato passed on it this time. Even without the additional pops of fruit, it was deliciously sweet. Amid the unseasonably hot weather and a feeling of fatigue after his morning pole dancing practice, the flavor was very refreshing.

In the end, it remains to be seen whether or not this brand can catch on in Japan, but for now, it appears that crowds are yet to form.

content:
Pikachu Sweets bakes up new treats to celebrate Pokémon’s 30th birthday.

This year marks the 30th anniversary of Pokémon, which is another way of saying it’s the franchise’s 30th birthday…and everyone knows you can’t celebrate a birthday without cake, right?

And if you’re looking for a cake to celebrate this particular birthday, there’s no more appropriate choice than a Pikachu cake.

That’s exactly what’s coming to Tokyo’s Pikachu Sweets by Pokémon Cafe next month. Not to be confused with the full-scale, sit-down Pokémon Cafe near Tokyo Station, Pikachu Sweets is a dessert stand located inside the Sunshine City shopping/entertainment complex in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro neighborhood.

Seen in these photos is the Poké-patissiers’ newest creation, the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich, made of two Pikachu-shaped slices of moist, fluffy shortcake with whipped cream and sliced strawberries between them, giving you a mix of sweet, tart, and milky flavors.

Served in a little celebratory paper holder, this is a shortcake you can eat without your hands without getting your fingers messy, and the raised corners of the holder should keep the cake securely in place as you raise it up to snap a photo before your first bite, maybe with the Pikachu Sweets storefront in the background.

Coming to the menu on the same day as the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich is a new dessert drink, the Eevee Chocolate Frappe, with an adorable Eevee Pokémon 30th anniversary cookie and a swirl of whipped cream sitting atop the slushy chocolate drink, creating a color pattern evocative of Eevee’s coat.

If you order a Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich plus an Eevee Chocolate Frappe or a Catch ‘Em Latte (“Get Latte” in Japanese) also gets you one of three 30th anniversary stickers with an illustration of a Pikachu wearing a cafe uniform.

The lattes come in four different varieties (caffe latte, tea latte, caffe mocha, or caramel latte), hot or cold, and they’ll also be getting 30th anniversary foam art.

The lineup goes on sale November 5 and will be available until December 31, with both the Pikachu cake and Eevee frappe priced at 1,200 yen (US$7.60).

Pikachu Sweets has no actual eat-in space, so customers generally either take their treats home or enjoy them on one of the benches within Sunshine City or in the adjacent outdoor plaza. The shop does caution, though, that because of the whipped cream, the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich won’t keep for very long once it’s taken out of its refrigerated showcase, so they advise against waiting until you get home to eat it, especially since the store doesn’t provide cool packs to keep the cake chilled, and so this is a case where the healthiest thing to do is not resist digging into your dessert promptly after you have it in your hands.

title: Super Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto to receive Order of Culture from Japanese emperor
description: If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him. Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture. These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and […]
content:
If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him.

Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture. These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and more.

And when it comes to people who made an impact on Japanese culture, I doubt there’s anyone who’d disagree that Shigeru Miyamoto belongs in that group. After creating one of the most influential games of its time, Donkey Kong, in 1983, he played a critical role in revitalizing the slumping global video game industry with Japan at its center through Super Mario Bros. in 1985, creating both a revolutionary style of game and iconic characters that would thrive for the next 40 years. And everything he’s done since then, such as contributions to classic franchises like Zelda, Mario Kart, Star Fox and Pikmin, is just a ton of thick, sweet icing on the cake.

In honor of this, Miyamoto will be presented the award by Emperor Naruhito at the Imperial Palace alongside seven other recipients, including Kenso Soai, who also won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry this year, and Shunichi Tokura, the composer of Pink Lady’s smash hit “UFO” and the current chair of JASRAC.

In a press conference following the announcement, Miyamoto said, “I am truly happy to have found video games. As a creator, I have just as much fun developing games as the players do playing them. It is a joy to be able to keep doing this.”

He also had the following advice for younger game designers: “I often tell them it is better not to start with a game they’re already a big fan of and find entertaining and just try to tweak it to make it ‘more fun.’ Instead of refining something that already exists, it is much more rewarding to start at the core and ask yourself, ‘Wouldn’t it be interesting if I tried this?’ Then focus your energy on building something from that idea.”

Miyamoto will also be the first person from the gaming industry to have received this honor. After the news broke, there was an outpouring of support and congratulations from people all over Japan in online comments.

“It’s long overdue, but wonderful news. Mario and Zelda are beloved not just in Japan but all over the world.”
“I make recipes but was happy to hear he feels the same joy in his work and always thinks ‘Wouldn’t this be interesting?’ like I do.”
“Even as the game market has grown to a huge scale, Mario and Zelda continue to rank among the top-sellers. He is a person who shaped countless lives all over the world.”
“His work influenced our youths, the way we spent time with our family, and some of our unforgettable memories.”
“Miyamoto never pandered to trends and always asked himself if his creations made people feel something.”
“When he started out, video games were seen negatively. Now, his characters have appeared at the Olympics!”
“I remember being completely hooked on Donkey Kong. I tried the famous shortcut trick over and over but could never do it!”
“Paul McCartney even asked for Miyamoto’s autograph when they met and greeted him by singing the Super Mario song.”

Speaking of Paul McCartney, it’d probably be fair to say that the next person from the game industry who should get an Order of Culture is none other than Koji Kondo, whose scores for Super Mario Bros. and Zelda were just as impactful and enduring as the games themselves.

title: Tokusatsu hero “Moonlight Mask’s” pocket change donations help traffic accidents victims in Japan
description: Small change and a big heart. A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask, a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping […]
content:
Small change and a big heart.

A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask, a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping out in other ways. Based on a wrestling manga hero of the same name, these real-life heroes have also led to a variety of copycats and spin-offs. I think there was even a kind-hearted Jason Mask one time.

And every New Year’s Eve since 1974, on Sado Island in Niigata Prefecture, police have discovered a bag full of coins at one of their stations and outposts, along with a note that reads, “These are coins I collected, one by one every day. I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little,” and is signed “Gekko Kamen,” meaning “Moonlight Mask” in English and also occasionally localized as “Moonbeam Man.”

Hardcore tokusatsu fans will likely know one or more of these names as the precursor to the entire genre of superhero kids TV shows. Originally airing in the ’50s, Moonlight Mask was the archetypal masked, motorcycle-riding crusader of justice.

Every year the police honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and donate the coins to funds supporting those orphaned by traffic accidents. However, very recently, something truly unexpected happened.

On 19 October, in Niigata City on the mainland of the prefecture, a police officer approached his patrol car and found an envelope on the windshield. Inside were coins totaling 240 yen (US$1.53), and on the envelope a note said, “I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little.”

On the same day, about 1.5 kilometers from the first incident, another envelope was found at a police box in the Shirone Chuo area of the city. This one contained 299 yen (US$1.99) in change and had a note with the very same legendary words of Moonlight Mask. In both cases, no witnesses spotted anyone leaving the envelopes. This would mark the first time in over 50 years that Moonlight Mask or someone else using the same moniker donated to victims of car accidents outside of Sado Island.

▼ News report showing the envelopes and coins

Deputy Chief Ryo Takahashi of the Niigata Minami Police Precinct said they will honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and forward the 539 yen to children orphaned by traffic accidents. He added, “I am deeply moved by this person’s unending concern for the victims of car accidents. Because they are a hero, we are not investigating to uncover their true identity.”

We can probably all agree that a noble deed should be respected regardless of its magnitude. However, this particular magnitude wasn’t enough to cover a combo at McDonald’s, and some readers of the news online had trouble fully coming to terms with that.

“Oh… Well…”
“I thought the report just had a typo in the number.”
“It is the thought that counts, I guess…”
“It’s always been New Year’s Eve. So why now?”
“He does donate often. I looked it up, and this is his 53rd donation. Last time he gave 30,010 yen.”
“I guess the rising cost of living is even putting a strain on Moonlight Mask.”
“I wonder if this person is extremely poor themself.”
“I want to say the amount isn’t important, but at a certain point wouldn’t this be considered a form of harassment?”
“Only a horrible person would laugh at a gesture like this.”
“This person must be pretty old by now. That was probably a good amount of money in their day.”
“Their handwriting is very neat. They must be very meticulous.”
“539 was the license plate number of Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle! Do your homework before shooting off your mouths!!!”

That last comment would have been a cool detail, but a fun fact is that Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle had the license plate number Mu-8323 or 8328. Though it can be hard to see with from the angles the TV series’ scenes were filmed at, and with 1950s-quality cameras, some eagle-eyed fans were able to catch a peek of the superhero’s road-legal bike and at least narrow it down to those two.

It’s especially ironic because while within the series private detective Juro Iwai is heavily implied to be Moonlight Mask’s secret identity, this is never confirmed, and even the actor for Moonlight Mask is listed as “?” in the credits. But anyone even remotely inclined to find out who he is need only look at the back of his bike and run a check on it.

It just goes to show that the true spirit of Moonlight Mask is to help those in need and right the wrongs of society at all costs, even if your plan isn’t all that well thought out. Every little bit helps.

title: Ghibli composer Joe Hisaishi named Composer-in-Residence of Los Angeles Philharmonic
description: Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences. At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to […]
content:
Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences.

At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to Studio Ghibli’s most beloved anime films, including My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away, since Hisaishi continues to display a boundless passion and enthusiasm for making music and sharing it with as wide an audience as possible.

For example, en route to setting a couple of Guinness World Records, he held a series of concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles over three days this past July. If you missed your chance to see him then, don’t worry, because Hisaishi has now been named Composer-in-Residence of the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra.

This isn’t some simple honorary title/goodwill ambassador deal either. The L.A. Phil is describing the relationship as “a five-year creative partnership” that will start with the upcoming 2027/2028 concert season. In addition to recurring performances at all three of the organization’s customary venues (the iconic hillside Hollywood Bowl, the adjacent John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, and the downtown Walt Disney Concert Hall), Hisaishi “will create new works specifically for the LA Phil and its audiences” while also engaging in new commissions, recording projects, and educational and community outreach endeavors.

“Los Angeles holds a special place in my musical life-from the premiere of my Harp Concerto with the LA Phil’s Emmanuel Ceysson at Walt Disney Concert Hall to our recent performances at the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford,” said Hisaishi following the announcement, and also that he’s “deeply honored” to be chosen for the role. “In the seasons ahead, I look forward to exploring new musical horizons with this extraordinary orchestra and sharing the spirit of discovery with audiences in Los Angeles and beyond.”

▼ An audio clip of one of Hisaishi’s previous Hollywood Bowl concerts

View this post on Instagram

▼ With Hisaishi scheduled to be spending a lot more time in L.A., he’ll also be able to check out America’s first One Piece store, should the mood strike him.

Hisaishi’s resume isn’t composed entirely of Ghibli soundtracks, as he’s also made contributed selected compositions or arrangements to other anime including Mobile Suit Gundam, Children of the Sea, Kimagure Orange Road, and Creamy Mami, as well as creating the soundtrack for video game Ni no Kuni and a handful of live-action Beat Takeshi movies. There’s no denying, though, that Hisaishi is most strongly associated with the work he’s done for Ghibli, As a matter of fact, there’s never been a Hayao Miyazaki-directed Ghibli feature film that Hisaishi didn’t write the score for, and with the studio’s track record of leaving a deep impression on fans around the world with its soundscapes, no doubt the new creative journey Hisaishi is about to embark on will be another movingly memorable one.

title: One of Tokyo’s most beautiful soft serve ice creams is also one of its trickiest to find [Photos]
description: Mr. Sato’s determination pays off in treat for the eyes and taste buds. Recently, our ace reporter Mr. Sato told us that he needed to go to Toranomon Hills, a shopping and entertainment complex in downtown Tokyo’s Toranomon neighborhood. Why? To eat ice cream. As Mr. Sato explained, recently he’s been seeing photo after photo […]
content:
Mr. Sato’s determination pays off in treat for the eyes and taste buds.

Recently, our ace reporter Mr. Sato told us that he needed to go to Toranomon Hills, a shopping and entertainment complex in downtown Tokyo’s Toranomon neighborhood. Why? To eat ice cream.

As Mr. Sato explained, recently he’s been seeing photo after photo of the soft serve ice cream from Dolce Tacubo, a dessert cafe located in Toranomon Hills, that’s been going viral. “Once the algorithm decides ‘You like this kind of stuff, don’t you?’ and starts filling your social feeds with it, you end up wanting to try it more and more, right?” he told us while heading out the door.

Honestly, we’ve never known Mr. Sato to need any prodding by outside forces to convince him to eat ice cream, but we trust his savvy sense when it comes to photogenic sweets, and we anxiously awaited his report…which almost didn’t come in.

Like a lot of Japanese shopping centers, Toranomon Hills has a food section, called T-Market, in its basement area. Mr. Sato assumed that’s where he’d find Dolce Tacubo, but after making multiple laps of the place, he still couldn’t find the cafe.

So next he took the elevator up to the higher levels of the building, but he still couldn’t find it. Even consulting Google Maps didn’t clear things up, since the app told him to exit the building entirely, then come back in through another entrance, which didn’t make any logical sense to him. Eventually, it was human intelligence that put him on the right path, as Mr. Sato asked the Toranomon Hills employee posted at the taxi stand where he could find Dolce Tacubo, and they informed him that the cafe really is the T-Market zone, on basement level 2, so back down the escalator our reporter went.

At the risk of offending the sensibilities of interior designers with a penchant for minimalism, T-Market’s aesthetics might be a little too elegant for their own good. A number of the understated storefronts don’t have the shop’s name prominently displayed above their entrances, which is how Mr. Sato managed to walk right past this place multiple times…

…before he finally realized this actually is Dolce Tacubo!

He’d been almost ready to give up and go home before he spotted the surprisingly unassuming sign for Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve, but now that he knew he was in the right place, it was time to try the viral-hit dessert for himself. The ice cream is available in three varieties, vanilla, kabocha/Japanese pumpkin, and “mixed,” which gives you both flavors together. The vanilla is 1,000 yen (US$6.30) and the kabocha 1,200, which are premium prices for ice cream in Japan, and it’s a little weird that the mixed cone is 1,300 yen, more expensive than an all-kabocha cone despite half of it being the less-expensive vanilla ice cream.

But hey, desserts aren’t always logical, so Mr. Sato decided to splurge on a mixed cone, and waited in the café’s eat-in space while the staff prepared his treat.

It was every bit as beautiful as he’d hoped it would be. Amazingly, the swirly ridges of vanilla and kabocha wound through and wrapped around each other without any smearing save for a small section at the very top.

The roasted pumpkin seeds are a classy touch too, and there’s so much care put into the presentation that it almost feels like personal pampering, putting a big smile on Mr. Sato’s face.

Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is more than just a proverbial pretty face, too. Both of the types of ice cream are rich and flavorful. If you’ve never had kabocha sweets before, they tend to be both lighter and sweeter than what you’d get with Western-style pumpkin pie, and this is an outstanding example of how well it can work as an ice cream flavor. In terms of texture Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is actually on the firmer end of the spectrum within the category, dense enough that you can easily stand a spoon in it when it’s just-served. It melts easily on the palate, though, and has a silky mouthfeel without any significant grittiness.

Mr. Sato can’t finish his taste-testing notes without mentioning the waffle cone too. It’s got a nice, substantial weight to it and a stimulating crunchiness that makes for some great synergy with the smooth ice cream.

Beautiful, delicious, and interesting, Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is a high-quality dessert by any metric, and Mr. Sato feels it definitely justifies not only its cost, but also the determination it might take to find it.

title: Japan’s newest tempura is…potato salad tempura?!? [Taste test]
description: Annual idea contest takes Tenya to a bold new tempura frontier. Tempura is one of the most versatile styles of Japanese cuisine, especially when it comes to vegetables. Onion, carrots, eggplant, and kabocha (Japanese pumpkin), to name just a few, all lend themselves to Japan’s traditional method of deep-frying, and they’re all things the staff […]
content:
Annual idea contest takes Tenya to a bold new tempura frontier.

Tempura is one of the most versatile styles of Japanese cuisine, especially when it comes to vegetables. Onion, carrots, eggplant, and kabocha (Japanese pumpkin), to name just a few, all lend themselves to Japan’s traditional method of deep-frying, and they’re all things the staff at tempura restaurant chain Tenya are happy to cook up on a daily basis.

Tenya’s chefs, though, are also always on the lookout for new things to try the tempura treatment on, and this month they’ve come up with one of their most surprising innovations yet: potato salad tempura.

This bold concept (arguably the boldest since Tenya created clam chowder tempura) is the winner of Tenya’s annual employee idea competition, but the chain realizes it might be too bold to make an entire meal out of. Instead, you’ll find the potato salad tempura as part of the new Azayaka Vegipote (“Vegetable Potato”) Tempura Bowl, which went on sale October 22. In addition to the tempura potato salad, you also get tempura eggplant, corn, bell pepper, zucchini, and radish.

If you’re wondering how Tenya manages to deep-fry something that doesn’t have a defined shape, the unique consistency of Japanese mayonnaise is probably a big help. Japanese mayo is a lot less watery than its western counterpart. That gives it enough density for the tempura batter to stick to without actually combining with the mayo, and as you can see in our mid-taste test photo below, Tenya really has succeeded in making tempura pouches with potato salad inside!

This results in an extremely interesting texture. The outer layer has the distinctive airy crunch that tempura fans love. Inside you’ve got the creamy mayo, softened by the heat but still not watery, and mixed in are slices of potato that crumble enticingly when you bite into them.

It’s extremely rare for a single piece of tempura to have that much going on in terms of texture, and it’s a very satisfying combination, as it turns out the flavors of potato salad and tempura complement each other extremely well too, our taste-testing reporter P.K. Sanjun reports. While he’s not sure it would work as a solo topping in the way that, say, a rice bowl topped with nothing but multiple pieces of tempura shrimp does, now that he knows how good it tastes, a piece of tempura potato salad would always be a welcome addition to his meal team, and especially in a vegetable tempura ensemble like this, it’s a great addition.

However, the tempura potato salad, and the 790-yen (US$5) Azayaka Vegipote bowl that it comes in, are currently only available on a limited-quantity basis, with a total of 8,000 to be served in its initial run, so if the idea sounds intriguing to you, you’ll want to head to Tenya ASAP, since there’s nowhere else to get tempura like this.

content:
Are you ready for a taste of terror?

As Universal Studios Japan marks its 25th anniversary, the park is bursting with thrills with its milestone 15th edition of Halloween Horror Nights. Running from September 11 to November 8, this year’s event pairs the classic street scares with an array of spook-filled food and drink offerings that make it well worth a visit.

The headliner for 2026’s new additions is the park’s first-ever Zombie Bar. Occupying Wharf Cafe in the San Francisco area of the park and operating nightly from 6:00 p.m., it features zombified crew members serving eerie signature drinks themed around past park monsters. Highlights include a strawberry-milk Cutie Zombie drink, a non-alcoholic lychee sour for circus zombie fans, and a blood orange and lemon sour inspired by chainsaw zombies.

▼ Cutie Zombie’s Sweet Temptation — Strawberry Milk

▼ Circus Zombie’s Madness: Lychee Non-Alcoholic Sour

▼ Chainsaw Zombie’s Rampage — Blood Orange & Lemon Sour

Over at Universal Market, high school zombies take the center stage with a creepy school festival theme. Visitors can enjoy blackcurrant waffles from the Zombie Cheerleading Club, garlic-oil experimental takoyaki from the Science Club, or a cheese and onion kalbi (Korean marinated beef ribs) rice dog designed by the ravenous American Football Club, with a night-exclusive banana ice cream to indulge in for dessert.

▼ #Deco Champion Zombie Cheer Squad Cassis Waffle

▼ Burst! Zombie Science Club Experimental Takoyaki — with Umami Garlic Oil

▼ Muscle Rampage! Zombie American Football Club’s Cheese Beef Kalbi Rice Sandwich

▼ Zombie Banana Ice — Does a Banana Count as a Snack?

Anime and gaming enthusiasts have a ton to look forward to as well, thanks to collaborations with Resident Evil and Chainsaw Man. Coinciding with the 30th anniversary of Resident Evil, known as “Biohazard” in Japan, a croissant sandwich filled with chicken, vegetables, and a green-herb basil sauce is offered to honor the new Resident Evil Requiem: The Dive maze, along with a bitter chocolate churro to pay homage to agent Leon S. Kennedy, both being sold at the food cart in front of Space Fantasy – The Ride and accompanied by some original merchandise.

▼ Green Herb Recovery Croissant Bun — Basil Sauce & Chicken and Leon S. Kennedy’s Dark Chocolate Churritos

Chainsaw Man fans should swing by the food cart near Cinema 4-D to pick up a keema curry Chainsaw Man Bun, expressing the transformed Denji, alongside an orange-vanilla Pochita frozen parfait, with Pochita’s posterior on full display as he digs into the dessert. Additionally, a full lineup of original goods will be unveiled in the Cinema 4-D store, such as T-shirts featuring Chainsaw Man fighting the Halloween Horror Nights Devil, and cute keychains of Pochita in a mummy costume.

title: Trial of terminally ill cancer patient who found 22 million yen on the street and kept it ends
description: Defendant described money as a “gift from God.” They say truth is stranger than fiction, but sometimes truth is exactly as strange as fiction. Such was the case of a 43-year-old man who, shortly after having the worst day of his life, suddenly had the best day of his life in a twist of fate […]
content:
Defendant described money as a “gift from God.”

They say truth is stranger than fiction, but sometimes truth is exactly as strange as fiction. Such was the case of a 43-year-old man who, shortly after having the worst day of his life, suddenly had the best day of his life in a twist of fate that might even be considered cliché if seen in a movie.

Earlier this year, the man, who lives in the city of Higashimatsushima, Miyagi Prefecture, was told that his cancer that had gone into remission was recurring, and he only had two or three months to live. He later described feeling as if he had given up on everything at that point and just wandered around aimlessly.

Not too long after that, at about noon on 5 March, a security crew was transporting the cash from a game center in the nearby city of Sendai. As they were loading it into an armored car, one of the guards dropped a bag, and they drove off without noticing it. Just then, the terminally ill man happened to be walking by and saw the satchel lying on the sidewalk.

▼ The area where the bag was found is rather busy.

He passed it at first, but curiosity got the better of him. He turned around, picked it up, and took it to a public restroom, where he pried it open with a craft knife to find 22 million yen (US$139,000) in cash. He said that at the time, he thought it “was a gift from God,” and for the next four and a half months, spent 18 million yen ($114,000) of the money on medical treatments and traveling abroad.

Naturally, the parties involved in losing the 22 million yen were determined to get it back. With the help of police, they eventually caught up with the man and arrested him for misappropriation of lost property in July.

On 19 October, his trial was held and lasted only one day, with the man admitting to the charges against him. In closing arguments, the prosecution described the man’s actions as “utterly selfish” and requested a one-year prison sentence, while the defense said that due to the man’s mental state at the time, a suspended sentence would be appropriate.

Sentencing is scheduled for 6 November, but the court of public opinion seems split on the matter of whether the man’s actions were excusable given his situation or a crime that deserves justice despite it.

“It wasn’t a gift from God. It was lost property, and he stole it.”
“I’d probably have done the same thing. It’s like something out of a manga.”
“It was the guards who lost the money. Can a judge really expect him to use sound judgment just after being told he was going to die?”
“He should have just turned it in. They probably would have given him a reward, and he could have enjoyed that guilt-free.”
“If I drop money on the street and someone takes it. I blame myself.”
“Is he even going to survive this trial?”
“I wonder if using the money on medical treatment helped.”
“Maybe the next gift from God will be a miracle cure. Then, he’ll have to work the rest of his life paying that money off.”

The firm in charge of transporting the money had the 22 million yen covered by insurance, and the man has already entered into an agreement with the insurance company to repay the money. According to the terms he must pay them 30,000 yen ($190) a month until the full amount is paid, which should take until sometime around the year 2076.

title: Japanese scientists developing cute, autonomously swarming robo dogs for anti-bear patrols [Video]
description: Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog. Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming […]
content:
Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog.

Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming wider in their search for stuff to eat,

With bear attacks having become a topic of heightened concern in recent years, and northern Japan having the country’s largest bear populations, earlier this year Akita Prefectural University began accepting proposals from faculty and students for its Bear-Tech Solution Contest. A total of 41 entries were submitted, and on October 13 a selection of the most promising ideas were presented in Akita City, including an idea for a surprisingly cute anti-bear robot dog.

Called Hacchan, the robot named after Japan’s most famous Akita Inu, Hachiko. Rather than hang out around Shibuya Station waiting for its master to come home and munching on grilled chicken handouts, though, Hacchan’s behavior is inspired by the Akita Inu hunting dogs that would accompany Akita Prefecture’s traditional huntsmen into the woods in days of yore.

▼ Hacchan can be seen at the point in the video queued here.

However, unlike actual hunting dogs, Hacchan has been created with a nonviolent outcome in mind. The quadrupedal robot is meant for deployment on the edge of farms or towns, and when its camera detects a bear, it uses an internal speaker to play the sound of a dog barking loudly in order to scare the animal off and make it retreat back into the woods. By sharing its location data, Hacchan can even call other units to the scene, creating a pack of robo dogs for a more intimidating presence, while also building a database of bear sighting and behavior to help the robots efficiently and autonomously patrol the outer edges of the community.

Researcher Masayuki Yoshida of the university’s Regional Collaboration and Research Promotion Center, who’s leading the development of Hacchan, says they hope to begin field testing the robot dogs before the end of the year.

title: Family Mart enters the soft serve game with giga-sized cones of milk or matcha goodness
description: Four stores in Tokyo recently started selling the soft serve in three flavors with little to no fanfare. Ministop is usually the Japanese convenience store chain that people equate with fresh soft serve ice cream, but that may be about to change now that one of The Big Three chains, Family Mart, seems to be […]
content:
Four stores in Tokyo recently started selling the soft serve in three flavors with little to no fanfare.

Ministop is usually the Japanese convenience store chain that people equate with fresh soft serve ice cream, but that may be about to change now that one of The Big Three chains, Family Mart, seems to be experimenting with soft serve at four locations in Tokyo. Strangely, however, we couldn’t find any official press release related to it on Family Mart’s website, and October seems like an odd time to unveil a frozen dessert. Perhaps the mystery is meant to be part of the allure…

Our very own zany reporter and sweets enthusiast Mr. Sato had gotten a hot tip that the Kanda Awaji-cho location is one of the stores offering soft serve. He headed over to check it out for himself and found an unassuming poster out front, but that was about it. He would have thought they would be making a bigger fuss of it.

The three flavors being offered are milk, matcha, and mix (milk & matcha). Each one is offered in a “short size” (250 yen/US$1.60) or “giga size” (298 yen) and can be ordered in a cup or cone.

▼ The giga size is pictured most prominently below, while the short size is pictured in milk flavor-form in the bottom left.

Orders for the soft serve should be placed at the counter, and there are handy ordering cards with each of the three flavors for you to hand over to the staff. Be sure to specify if you’d like a short size, as giga seems to be the default.

Mr. Sato of course sprung for the giga size, and it was ready quite quickly. Here was his first-ever Family Mart soft serve cone!

It started melting right away so he quickly snapped a couple of photos and dug in. It was a rich, creamy milk flavor with moderate sweetness and the perfect full-bodied texture inside his mouth.

He had the feeling that Ministop’s milky flavor is a bit more prominent, though he can’t confirm that without trying them side by side.

▼ Regardless, he’ll scream for ice cream no matter what!

Rumors are that Family Mart hopes to sell the soft serve at four more stores in the Tokyo area by the end of the year as well, bringing the total to eight stores. Mr. Sato is happy as long as there’s an increasing number of opportunities to find convenience store soft serve moving forward–and he’ll keep supporting Ministop, too!

title: America is getting its first-ever One Piece store, and the opening date has been revealed!
description: The Straw Hat Pirates sail into the City of Angels with cool California-exclusive merch. The hearts of otaku were dealt a painful blow this week when visa problems lead to the sudden cancellation of two Umamusume concerts in Los Angeles, which were supposed to be the franchise’s first musical performances on American soil. content:
The Straw Hat Pirates sail into the City of Angels with cool California-exclusive merch.

The hearts of otaku were dealt a painful blow this week when visa problems lead to the sudden cancellation of two Umamusume concerts in Los Angeles, which were supposed to be the franchise’s first musical performances on American soil. It’s not all bad news for anime fans in the City of Angels, though, as the opening date has been announced for the first-ever permanent One Piece specialty store in the U.S.!

It’s not going to be stuck in the back corner of some random strip mall, either. The One Piece Mugiwara Store will be waiting for visitors inside downtown Los Angeles’ Westfield Century City shopping mall on Santa Monica Boulevard, right down the street from Beverly Hills.

▼ Mugiwara is the Japanese word for “straw,” as in “Straw Hat Pirates”

The shop will be opening on November 6, stocked with a wide variety of One Piece merch, featuring both items imported from Japan and exclusive items that aren’t available anywhere else, even at the One Piece Mugiwara Store branches in Japan, such as apparel items with a California license plate motif, surfer-version Chopper, or the message “I love LA” with an Op-Op Fruit in place of a heart.

The Surfer Chopper design was created specially for the L.A. store, and will also feature in some sort of interactive in-store experience that includes audio messages for visitors to hear.

View this post on Instagram

▼ Figure,s furoshiki wrapping cloths, and a whole lot of blind-buy trinkets will be among the items imported from Japan.

With the One Piece anime debuting 27 years ago, and the manga two years before that, there should be plenty of pent-up demand among American fans for an entire shop dedicated to the series, and as a crowd control measure, reservations will be necessary to enter the One Piece Mugiwara Store between November 6 and 12, and can be made through the shop’s official website here.
